artifacts.synopsis: TE John Evans appealed Arizona Presbytery's vote to divest him of his office without censure under BCO 34-10, after he had already affiliated with the Evangelical Presbyterian Church in England and Wales and notified the Presbytery of his withdrawal. The SJC unanimously sustained the appeal and reversed the Presbytery's action, holding that Evans had withdrawn from Presbytery's jurisdiction under BCO 38-3a before the divestiture proceedings began, and instructed the Presbytery to record the irregularity, acknowledge his new membership, and remove his name from the roll.

artifacts.title: Myers v. Illiana Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: TE Aaron Myers appealed Illiana Presbytery's decision to elevate his censures from indefinite suspension from office and from the Sacraments to excommunication and deposition, without any additional judicial process. The SJC sustained the appeal 21-1, holding that due process principles require some form of process before censure may be elevated, though the majority held that full de novo judicial process was not required; the sole dissent (RE Eggert) argued that Traditional Process under the BCO Rules of Discipline was required, and a concurring opinion (Sartorius) also argued for full BCO process.

artifacts.title: Benyola v. Central Florida Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC found the complaint administratively out of order because Mr. Benyola was no longer a member of any PCA congregation and thus lacked standing. The SJC approved the dismissal unanimously 23-0.

artifacts.title: Harrell et al. v. Covenant Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Seven members of a PCA mission church were tried and censured by a provisional Session for opposing the organizing minister's continuation as permanent pastor. The SJC sustained the appeal and reversed the convictions, holding that the indictments lacked required specificity under BCO 32-5, that the accused had no sinned against the fifth or ninth commandment by expressing opinions about ministerial suitability, and that the right to choose a pastor belongs to the congregation—not the provisional Session. A concurring opinion addressed indictment requirements, standard of review in appeals, and congregational rights in mission church minister selection.

artifacts.title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC sustained the complaint, ruling that a Session erred by prescreening and eliminating a deacon's nomination for ruling elder before the mandatory instruction and examination process required by BCO 24-1. The decision held that BCO 24-1's language is mandatory and that sessions cannot add a preliminary vetting step that bypasses the required sequence of instruction and examination.

artifacts.title: Evans and Pitts et al. v. Arizona Presbytery

The SJC sustained the complaints of Evans and Pitts et al., annulled the deposition, and remanded the matter to AZP for action consistent with BCO 38-1 requirements; a lengthy concurring opinion by RE Donahoe extensively analyzed BCO 38-1 confession procedures.

The SJC dismissed the complaint as judicially out of order (11-9-2-2) on the ground that Doty lacked standing under BCO 43-1 as a non-member of Nashville Presbytery; a significant dissent argued that her filing of charges gave her standing under prior precedent (Lyons, Ruff, Fordice).

artifacts.synopsis: TE Stuart Merriam, a minister transferred from PCUSA to Tennessee Valley Presbytery in 1986, was subject to ecclesiastical discipline based on his criminal conviction in Papua New Guinea. The SJC sustained Merriam's appeal, finding that TVP violated due process principles and procedures under the BCO, particularly by failing to appoint counsel and conducting an inadequate trial. The case was remanded to TVP for a new trial following proper BCO procedures.

artifacts.synopsis: Bruce Nickoley and David Stephens complained against Southwest Presbytery's actions in withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving a pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of a local church session. The SJC denied the complaint, affirming that the Presbytery correctly determined it lacked constitutional authority to suspend the session or act as a 'Session pro tem' without congregational consent, and that original jurisdiction over charges against ruling elders rested with the local session.
